memory: Another significant benefit of research is the opportunity to connect with professors on a more personal level. My principal investigator(PI) is incredibly approachable, and I can easily pop into her office to discuss anything from career direction to academic struggles. She's been instrumental in recommending me for various scholarships, events, and networking opportunities. I recently had the chance to attend a virtual workshop on immersive analytics, which brought together academic experts from around the world. Witnessing them debate technical details, propose new frameworks, and engage in light-hearted banter over rival theories was truly fascinating. It felt like I was experiencing the cutting-edge of CS knowledge in real time.That's a summary of my journey in the research world so far. It's been a lot of hard work, often more chaotic than expected, but also incredibly rewarding. I love the feeling that what I do in the lab might contribute to scientists understanding their data in a new way five or ten years down the line. Maybe one day the VR and immersive technologies we're pioneering will become standard tools, and I'll be able to look back and say, 'I was part of that from the beginning.' It's the sense of contributing to something bigger that keeps me motivated. Whether or not I decide to pursue a graduate degree soon, this experience has changed how I think about computer science, innovation, and teamwork. I couldn't imagine my undergraduate years without it—it's definitely enriched my perspective on what it means to be a computer scientist.I'm glad you mentioned that. As a fourth-year Computer Science student, I've had the opportunity to explore various communities on campus and get involved in different ways beyond just coding. It's great to see how the campus culture has evolved over the years and how there are so many ways to engage with the community. It really makes this place feel like a second home.I'm glad you shared that. Joining the Computer Science Society was a great decision for me. It's a wonderful community where we discuss new technologies, share personal projects, and often have industry speakers. It's a very welcoming environment, even for beginners. I've found that I can always learn from my fellow members, especially when it comes to topics like concurrency or containerization. They often have valuable insights from their internship experiences. It's been a fantastic way to expand my knowledge and network beyond the classroom.I'm really glad you mentioned the VR/AR Club. It's been a fantastic outlet for me to explore immersive analytics and connect with others who share my passion. The club is incredibly hands-on, with a dedicated VR lab in the engineering building equipped with cutting-edge hardware and innovative prototypes. We regularly host demos where members showcase their latest projects, ranging from engaging mini-games to more experimental applications like augmented reality interfaces for everyday tasks. I was particularly inspired by a recent demo of an AR tutor for advanced math, which used phone-based AR to provide interactive hints and 3D demonstrations. The enthusiasm and creativity among the members is truly motivating, and I feel lucky to be part of such a supportive community.I'm glad you mentioned the student-run radio station. I've had the chance to attend some of their open-mic nights, which are always a lot of fun. It's great to see people showcasing their talents in different ways, whether it's through music, poetry, or comedy. I remember one night when a friend from my Distributed Systems class performed an acoustic set. It was amazing to see him come alive on stage, sharing his soulful voice with the audience. Moments like that remind me that there's often more to someone than what you might see in a classroom or group project setting. It's wonderful to have these opportunities to discover new sides of our peers.I'm glad you mentioned the central lawn. It's a hub of activity on campus, with student organizations setting up booths and promoting their events. You can find everything from a cappella groups to environmental activism societies represented there. They often offer freebies like stickers or candy to attract new members. As a student, it's hard to resist the temptation of free pizza, so when a club includes that in their advertisement, I'm usually hooked. The lawn is also where some of the biggest campus events take place, such as our annual Tech Fest. During Tech Fest, project teams showcase their prototypes, and recruiters often attend in search of innovative ideas. It's a major event, especially for engineering and CS students. It's a great way to connect with like-minded individuals and stay updated on the latest trends in technology.I'm really glad you mentioned the campus hackathon. It was a truly eye-opening experience for me in my second year. Thousands of students from different backgrounds came together for 24 or 36 hours straight, hacking away in the student center. It was chaotic, but it was also exhilarating to see everyone's passion and creativity on display. I remember seeing beginners learning the basics of GitHub while advanced teams used complex machine learning libraries to achieve real-time image recognition. The atmosphere was electric, with sponsors and mentors roaming around to offer help whenever needed. I formed a small team with a few casual acquaintances, and the bond we formed during that all-nighter was unlike anything I'd experienced before. Sharing stale pizza at 3 a.m., debugging code, and cheering each other on created a sense of camaraderie that I'll always cherish. That's the essence of campus life: we're all in this together, forging friendships through shared experiences and challenges.I'm glad you shared that. Living in the engineering dorm, also known as "The Engi-House," was an incredible experience. The late-night coding sessions in the common lounge were legendary. You'd have someone working on an assignment for Data Structures while another group would be streaming e-sports tournaments. It was a high-intensity environment, but it also meant that if you encountered a stumbling block, there was always someone nearby who could offer a quick pointer. Beyond academics, we'd have potlucks, watch Netflix together, or even host a small talent show to blow off steam. It was a great way to build camaraderie and create lasting memories with my fellow engineers.I'm really glad you mentioned the "Tech for Good" day. It's been an incredibly rewarding experience for me to volunteer at these outreach events, especially when it comes to inspiring the next generation. The "Tech for Good" day is a fantastic initiative where local high school students come to campus to learn about programming and problem-solving. I've had the opportunity to run mini-workshops on topics like web development and basic Python. Seeing the younger students light up when they create a simple game or animated webpage is truly heartwarming. It brings back memories of when I was in their shoes, feeling overwhelmed by the vast world of technology. By providing them with a positive first experience, I feel proud to be making a difference. These events showcase a different side of campus life, highlighting the importance of community engagement and inspiring the next generation to pursue STEM fields. It's a wonderful way to contribute to the community and make a lasting impact.I'm glad you mentioned the social scene. While Greek life is present on campus, I've found that specialized clubs are a great way to meet people who share your interests. My friend who's into robotics joined the Robotics Team in his first semester and has since found a close-knit group of friends who share his passion. They spend their weekends together, watch movies, and grab dinner. Similarly, I've formed strong bonds with members of the VR/AR Club and the CS Society. We don't just talk about tech when we're together; we also enjoy joking around, complaining about cafeteria food, or planning weekend trips to the local hiking trails. It's a great way to balance academics with socializing and create lasting friendships.I'm really glad you mentioned Senior Week. It's a special tradition on campus that marks the end of our undergraduate journey. It's a series of events leading up to graduation, including a formal dance, a carnival, and a day where seniors get their photos taken in caps and gowns at iconic campus landmarks. I've heard it's a bittersweet experience, as it's the last hurrah before we scatter. My older friends who graduated last year said it was one of the best weeks of their college life, filled with laughter, nostalgia, and a touch of sadness that the journey was coming to an end. I'm both excited and a little anxious for it. After four years of making memories and creating lasting bonds, it's hard to believe that it's almost time to say goodbye to this chapter of my life. I'm looking forward to embracing the nostalgia and making the most of this special week.I'm glad you mentioned the Rivalry Game. It's a highly anticipated event on campus, with our sports teams facing off against our biggest rival college in various sports. While I'm not a die-hard sports fan, I absolutely love the electric atmosphere that week. Students and alumni alike show their school spirit by donning school colors, painting their faces, and waving banners. The night before the big football game, we often have a massive pep rally with fireworks, adding to the excitement. Even if you don't attend the game itself, the campus is filled with a contagious energy. Friends gather in dorm lounges or local bars to watch and cheer together. Whether we win or lose, the celebrations or commiserations can last all weekend, bringing everyone together across different majors and interests. It's a truly unifying moment for our campus community.
